note: Bundled retrieval corpus: 36 original short docs across 6 categories (defi, nft, security, wallets, layer2, mev). Self-written to stay leakage-free.

docs.title: Automated market makers
docs.text: Automated market makers replace order books with liquidity pools. Users deposit pairs of tokens into a pool, and a constant product formula prices trades. Larger pools mean less slippage, and liquidity providers earn a share of every swap fee. Market makers are permissionless, so anyone can add liquidity or trade at any time. The pool ratio shifts with every trade, which is how prices adjust without an exchange.

docs.title: Flash loans
docs.text: Flash loans let anyone borrow huge amounts with zero collateral, as long as the loan is repaid inside the same transaction. If repayment fails, the entire transaction reverts. Arbitrageurs use flash loans to equalize prices across exchanges without holding capital. Attackers use them to amplify exploits, because the capital needed for an attack drops to zero. Any protocol that assumes attackers are capital-constrained must enforce its invariants in code instead.

docs.title: Yield vaults
docs.text: Yield vaults pool deposits and run strategies that earn yield automatically. Vaults issue shares that represent a claim on the underlying assets, and the share price rises as the vault earns. Depositors can enter and exit at any time, subject to strategy limitations. Tokenized vault standards make it easy for wallets and aggregators to integrate any vault. The strategy is the risk: a clever but untested strategy can lose what the underlying asset could have earned.

docs.title: Stablecoins
docs.text: Stablecoins aim to hold a steady value, usually one dollar. Collateral-backed stables lock reserves in custody or in on-chain vaults and mint tokens against them. Overcollateralization absorbs price swings, and liquidation keeps the peg intact under stress. Algorithmic stablecoins without backing have historically collapsed when confidence dropped. A stablecoin is only as stable as its collateral, its oracles, and its redemption mechanism.

docs.title: Governance tokens and DAOs
docs.text: Governance tokens give holders voting power over a protocol. Proposals can change fees, upgrade contracts, or spend the treasury, and votes run over a fixed window. Many protocols add timelocks so users can exit before a change executes. Voting power concentrates in whales and delegates, which makes governance susceptible to capture. Lending markets can even be used to borrow tokens just to vote, so mature protocols checkpoint voting power against long-held positions.

docs.title: DeFi composability
docs.text: DeFi applications compose like Lego bricks: lend collateral in one app, borrow a stablecoin in a second, swap it in a third, and farm yield in a fourth. Every integration multiplies surface area. A bug in any contract can drain funds from every protocol that trusts it, often within one transaction. Composability is the source of DeFi's innovation and its sharpest risk. Integration audits and emergency mechanisms are the price of playing with bricks.

docs.title: NFT token standards
docs.text: NFT standards define how unique assets move on-chain. ERC-721 represents one-of-one assets like art and collectibles, with a unique id per token. ERC-1155 bundles fungible and non-fungible items in one contract, which saves gas in games with common and rare items. Choosing the right standard matters: wallets batch-transfer fungible balances but treat NFTs individually.

docs.title: Gaming NFTs
docs.text: Games use NFTs for items, characters, and land. ERC-1155 dominates gaming because a single contract can hold thousands of types of items, some with multiple copies and some one-of-one. Balances update per item type, so minting a weapon adds to its count instead of spawning a new contract. Games face the cold-start problem: an item is worthless until the game has players, and players leave if items are valueless.

docs.title: NFT royalties
docs.text: Royalties pay creators a percentage of every secondary sale. Traditional marketplaces enforced royalties by policy, but competing venues made them optional, and creator income dropped. On-chain royalty enforcement at the transfer level is being standardized so contracts can collect regardless of marketplace. The trade-off is flexibility: mandatory transfer fees complicate airdrops, games, and legitimate transfers.

docs.title: NFT metadata storage
docs.text: An NFT token is a pointer; the art usually lives elsewhere. Metadata can sit on centralized servers, on IPFS, or fully on-chain. If the pointer breaks, the token remains but the art is gone. Centralized URLs are the cheapest and most fragile; IPFS is content-addressed but depends on pinning; fully on-chain storage survives everything but costs gas. Serious collections treat metadata durability as a design requirement.

docs.title: NFT lending
docs.text: NFT lending lets owners borrow against their collectibles. Floor-price loans price a collection by its cheapest listing, while individual loans appraise a specific token. Liquidity is the constant problem: an NFT has no guaranteed market, so liquidations must handle slow exits. Collateral ratios are set wide to absorb price shocks. Culture collides with finance here more than anywhere else in crypto.

docs.title: Generative art mints
docs.text: Generative art collections mint thousands of variants from a script. Traits like background, body, and accessories combine deterministically, and rarity comes from how rarely a trait appears. Randomness on-chain is a security concern: weak randomness can be predicted or reverted until the minter gets a favorable output. Fair minting designs hide the random seed until after the purchase is committed.

docs.title: Reentrancy attacks
docs.text: Reentrancy happens when a contract calls an external contract before updating its own state. The attacker's contract re-enters the victim during the call and repeats the withdrawal before balances are marked as spent. The classic fix is checks-effects-interactions: validate, update state, then call out. Reentrancy guards are a safety net, but the ordering discipline is the real defense. Modern audits treat every external call as a potential re-entry point.

docs.title: Access control
docs.text: Access control decides who may call which function. A missing modifier can let any wallet withdraw the treasury, pause the protocol, or mint tokens. Common patterns are Ownable for a single admin and role-based access control for granular permissions. Functions that move funds or change parameters must be treated as the crown jewels. Reviewers check ownership transfers, initialization, and whether admin keys are themselves protected by a multisig.

docs.title: Oracle manipulation
docs.text: Price oracles feed off-chain prices into on-chain logic. A manipulable oracle lets attackers trade against a fake price: borrow against inflated collateral, liquidate innocent users at the wrong threshold, or drain a derivative. Single-source and spot-price oracles are the easiest to move, especially with flash loans. Defenses include time-weighted averages, multiple sources, deviation guards, and minimum liquidity requirements.

docs.title: Upgradeable contracts and timelocks
docs.text: Upgradeable contracts split storage and logic behind a proxy. The proxy delegates calls to an implementation, so the code can be swapped without moving funds. Delegation is powerful and dangerous: a bug in the upgrade path can brick the protocol or hand control to an attacker. Timelocks force a public delay before upgrades execute, giving users time to inspect and exit. Admin keys should rotate through a multisig and eventually dissolve.

docs.title: Approval phishing
docs.text: Approvals let contracts spend a user's tokens up to a limit. Phishing sites ask for approvals that look innocent, then drain everything the allowance covers. The least-privilege rule applies: approve only the exact amount needed for one transaction, then revoke. Wallets that surface the exact impact of a signature have cut losses sharply. Allowance sprawl across old contracts is why hygiene tools keep appearing.

docs.title: Invariants and audits
docs.text: Invariant tests assert properties that must always hold: total supply equals the sum of balances, the fee never exceeds a cap, or collateral always exceeds debt. Fuzzing tries millions of inputs to break invariants, and static analyzers scan the source for known vulnerability patterns. Manual review traces state transitions by hand. Audits are point-in-time; invariants are the living specification that keeps guarding the code as it changes.

docs.title: Seed phrases
docs.text: The seed phrase is the master key of a wallet. Twelve or twenty-four words derived from a well-known standard can regenerate every address and private key the wallet has ever used. Anyone holding the phrase owns everything under it, so it must never be photographed, typed into websites, or stored online. The phrase is not a password; it is the money itself.

docs.title: Hardware wallets
docs.text: Hardware wallets keep private keys inside a secure chip that never touches the internet. Transactions are signed on-device, and the computer only sees the signature. This defeats most remote malware because the key never leaves the device. Hardware devices still depend on the screen: a user must verify the exact address and amount before confirming. A hardware wallet protects keys, not judgment.

docs.title: Multisig wallets
docs.text: A multisig wallet requires a quorum of signatures before any transaction executes, like three out of five signers. Teams use multisigs so no single compromised key can drain the treasury. The trade-off is operational friction: every payment needs coordination, and a lost signer can freeze funds. Modern multisigs add spending limits, session keys for small transactions, and recovery paths for lost signers.

docs.title: Account abstraction
docs.text: Account abstraction turns wallets into programmable smart accounts. Instead of a bare keypair, an account can define its own validation: sponsored gas, gas paid in any token, spending limits, sessions, and multi-factor rules. User operations separate intent from execution: a user signs an intent and any executor can bundle and submit it. This is how crypto apps onboard users who never touch a native token.

docs.title: Social recovery
docs.text: Social recovery lets wallet owners name guardians who can jointly restore access. If the main key is lost or stolen, guardians vote to rotate in a new key after a delay. The delay is a shield: an attacker who steals a key still faces the wait, and the owner can use the delay to cancel the attempt. Recovery shifts the trust model from a secret to a circle of people.

docs.title: Allowance hygiene
docs.text: Every approval your wallet signs is a standing invitation to spend. Old approvals to abandoned contracts and test apps are the quiet risk in every wallet. The hygiene loop is simple: approve the minimum, transact, then revoke. Allowance dashboards surfaced billions of dollars in standing approvals on mainnet. A monthly revoke pass costs minutes and removes years of accumulated exposure.

docs.title: Rollups explained
docs.text: Rollups execute transactions off the main chain and post compressed data back to it. The main chain becomes the settlement and availability layer, which is why rollups inherit its security. Users see lower fees and faster confirmations while the security model stays anchored to Ethereum. The two families differ in how they prove correctness: optimistic rollups assume and challenge, zero-knowledge rollups prove and settle.

docs.title: Optimistic rollups
docs.text: Optimistic rollups assume state transitions are valid unless someone challenges them. A sequencer orders transactions and posts state roots. Watchers check the posted roots, and anyone can submit a fraud proof showing a transition was wrong. The challenge window is why withdrawals take days: the system waits long enough that fraud can be caught. Fast exit markets let users bridge out sooner by paying a fee.

docs.title: Zero-knowledge rollups
docs.text: Zero-knowledge rollups post a validity proof with every batch, proving the transition was computed correctly. There is no challenge window, so withdrawals can be near-instant and finality is crisp. The cost moves to proof generation, which needs real hardware for large batches. Recursive proofs let rollups verify other rollups, which is how the ecosystem plans to scale beyond single chains.

docs.title: Bridges
docs.text: Bridges move assets between chains by locking tokens on the source and minting equivalents on the destination. The peg is only as strong as whoever validates it: federated groups of signers, smart contract logic, or source-chain proofs. Bridge hacks dominate crypto losses because bridges concentrate value behind a single failure point. Canonical bridges that verify source-chain consensus directly are the safest pattern, and the safest bridge is still the one you do not need.

docs.title: Sequencers
docs.text: The sequencer is the party that orders transactions in a rollup. Users send transactions to the sequencer instead of the public mempool, and the sequencer commits ordered batches to the base layer. A centralized sequencer is fast but is a single point of trust and a censorship surface. Decentralized sequencing, shared ordering, and inclusion lists are active research areas; for now, most rollups run one sequencer with escape hatches.

docs.title: Finality
docs.text: Finality is the moment a transaction is guaranteed to stay. On a proof-of-stake base layer, finality arrives after a set number of blocks and validators agree. On optimistic rollups, transactions are effectively final only after the challenge window passes, because a fraud proof can still overturn them. Zero-knowledge rollups get near-immediate finality from their validity proofs. Always ask which finality a bridge or app is promising.

docs.title: What is MEV
docs.text: Maximal extractable value is profit captured by controlling transaction order. Block producers, validators, and searchers can reorder, include, or exclude transactions to extract value from them. Some extraction is healthy, like liquidating underwater loans; some is harmful, like sandwiching user trades. MEV is an economic property of blockchains, not a bug: the design question is who gets to capture it and under what rules.

docs.title: Sandwich attacks
docs.text: A sandwich attack surrounds a victim's trade. The attacker buys the token just before the victim's swap lands, pushing the price up, then sells right after, capturing the difference. The victim receives a worse price than the market offered. The attack needs monitoring the mempool and enough capital to move the price. Shorter block times, private mempools, and batch auctions all erode the sandwich.

docs.title: Frontrunning
docs.text: Frontrunning happens when a searcher sees a pending transaction, copies it, and pays more gas so their version lands first. Classic targets are trades, mints, and airdrop claims. The victim's transaction executes at the moved price; the frontrunner profits or simply steals the opportunity. Commit-reveal schemes hide the contents of a trade, and private transactions bypass the public mempool entirely. Frontrunning is the purest form of priority-as-payment.

docs.title: Liquidations
docs.text: Liquidations keep lending protocols solvent. When a borrower's collateral value falls below the required ratio, anyone can repay part of the debt and claim the collateral plus a bonus. Searchers race to liquidate first, which is legitimate competition that protects the protocol's funds. The danger is liquidation cascades under extreme volatility, when many positions cross the threshold at once. Protocol parameters like liquidation thresholds directly set the size of this race.

docs.title: Private order flow
docs.text: Private order flow delivers transactions directly to block producers, bypassing the public mempool where bots watch. Users gain protection from frontrunning and sandwiches; the operator usually takes a fee or shares the extracted value. Order flow auctions sell the right to order a bundle, and the proceeds often subsidize protocol revenue. Privacy for order flow is asymmetric: the user's trade hides from bots but is fully visible to whoever wins the auction.

docs.title: MEV on rollups
docs.text: Rollups change the MEV landscape. With a single sequencer, the traditional public-mempool race disappears because there is no public pool to watch. The sequencer itself becomes the orderer, so MEV moves to the operator level, and users depend on the sequencer's ordering policy. Preconfirmations let users pay for ordering promises, and shared sequencers aim to centralize ordering across many rollups. Each design shifts who captures value.
